newsitem.title: PERU: Peru special forces ready to end hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru special forces ready to end hostage crisis.

text.p: Crack Peruvian forces have been training for a possible storming of the besieged Japanese embassy residence in case negotiations for the release of about 340 hostages fail, police sources said on Sunday.
One source told Reuters that an assault would be undertaken as a last resort and emphasised that the military preparations were normal in a case like this one.
Famous for his hardline stance against Peru's rebels, President Alberto Fujimori has not ruled out using force to end the crisis, though aides claim he prefers a peaceful solution.
He told the Marxist hostage-takers on Saturday night in a tough television message that the only certain way to avoid bloodshed was to surrender their arms and hand over all the captives unharmed.

One police source said a storming of the residence would require 10 commandos to deal with each of the roughly 20 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels inside. It would last between three and five minutes, he added.
Peruvian security experts said that past experience of this type of assault indicated that it could result in deaths or injuries to about 20 percent of the hostages.
Any commando raid on the elegant two-story embassy residence would be a tough task, they added.
The windows are barred and protected by thick wire mesh and the building is surrounded by a high perimeter wall which special forces would need to cross to reach their target.
At least four of the guerrillas are rifle-toting marksmen stationed at second floor windows with telescopic night vision sights, police added.

Their muscular young comrades possess a small armory of AKM assault rifles, explosives, grenades and pistols. Released hostages have said the guerrillas have booby-trapped the entrances with explosives.
Peruvian commandos would also have to do without the help of the present or former heads of the anti-terrorism police DINCOTE, who are among the hostages.
Captive Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, speaking by walkie-talkie with local television from the residence on Saturday, described the rebels as well-armed and highly trained.
Security forces say the guerrillas are used to arduous conditions, having practiced prior to the assault in the tropical jungle of the Huallaga valley in northeast Peru.
Police say foreign former rebels probably helped train the MRTA, including ex-members of Colombia's M-19 movement, El Salvador's FMLN and Chile's MIR.
They have identified the leader of the hostage-takers as a 43-year-old Peruvian former factory worker named Nestor Cerpa.
Most of the guerrillas are Peruvian but there have been unconfirmed reports that some of the rebels speak Spanish with foreign accents.
Britain and the United States have sent security advisers to Lima in case their assistance is required; however, Fujimori has said he does not need any help.
